name: Pale Yellow-Green
lede: Pale Yellow-Green is a light, soft green leaning to yellow, a systematic name from Ridgway's color plates rather than a pigment or a plant.

sections.title: A systematic name
sections.body:
The phrase belongs to the descriptive tradition of naming colors by hue, lightness and strength. Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature has the swatch as plate VI, hue 31, in a light tone, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 119, "light yellow green", 4.5 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [1]. Our library finds no earlier record than 1912 [1].

Books use the words loosely. St Clair glosses [[chartreuse]] as a pale yellow-green, taking the name from the liqueur of the Carthusian monks [2]. The Pigment Compendium gives the same description to anhydrous nickel phosphate, a pale yellow-green pigment that needs heating to red heat to make [3].

sections.title: The color of distance
sections.body:
Gage records a seventeenth-century scheme of aerial perspective by the painter Zaccolini [4]. Colors fade toward the blue of the atmosphere in a set order, which he gave as black, green, "pale" (a yellow-green), purple, tan, red, yellow and white [4].

It sits beside [[light-green]] and [[moss-green]] in any palette of spring foliage.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 25 works, or 0.11 per cent, which is rarer than 64 per cent of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1800s, at 0.1 per cent of the 8,345 paintings from that century (9 paintings), 1.5 times the expected rate [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light [5]. The earliest match is a Carracci of about 1590 [5].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so these matches are look-alike hues, not proof of any pigment [5].

disambiguation.gloss: a brighter named green, also called a pale yellow-green

Zaccolini's perspective scale put a pale yellow-green third in the order of colors fading into haze.
